questions.question: What values can an indicator random variable take?
options: All real numbers
Only positive integers
Only values in $(0,1)$

questions.question: What is $\mathbf 1_A(\omega)$ when $\omega\notin A$?
options: $\omega$

questions.question: What does an indicator random variable do conceptually?
options: It turns an event into a numerical variable
It turns a random variable into an event only
It assigns probabilities to all intervals
It counts permutations

questions.question: What is the expectation of an indicator random variable?
options: The variance of the event
The probability of the event it indicates
The number of outcomes in the event
The probability of the complement of the indicated event

questions.question: If $A$ is the event that a customer returns a product, what does $\mathbf 1_A=1$ mean?
options: The customer does not return the product
The return probability is zero
The product has no price
The customer returns the product

questions.question: In occupancy problems, what can an indicator for a box being nonempty record?
options: $1$ if the box is nonempty and $0$ otherwise
The exact number of all boxes always
The probability of every arrangement
The size of the sample space

questions.question: In network reliability, what might a component indicator equal?
options: The total number of network paths
The variance of all components
The arrival time of a signal
$1$ if the component works and $0$ otherwise

questions.question: If two event indicators are summed, what can the sum represent?
options: The product of their probabilities only
A continuous density
A fixed nonrandom value always
How many of the two events occur

questions.question: Why is an indicator closely related to a Bernoulli random variable?
options: It is always normally distributed
It has support on all real numbers, like a normally distributed variable
It takes values $0$ and $1$ according to whether an event occurs
It cannot have an expectation

questions.question: Why does $E[\mathbf 1_A]=P(A)$?
options: The event $A$ must be certain
The indicator has variance zero
The complement of $A$ has probability zero, so the indicator always equals $1$
The indicator contributes $1$ exactly on $A$ and $0$ outside $A$

questions.question: If $A$ and $B$ occur but $C$ does not, what is $\mathbf 1_A+\mathbf 1_B+\mathbf 1_C$?
If $P(A)=0.8$, what is the expected value of the customer-return indicator for $A$?
If $I_i$ indicates whether box $i$ is nonempty, what does $\sum_i I_i$ count?
options: The number of empty boxes only
The probability that all boxes are empty
The maximum box label
The number of nonempty boxes

questions.question: What link do indicator random variables create between events and expectation?
options: They turn every event into a $0/1$ random variable with mean $1/2$
They let event probabilities be handled through expectations
They make $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$ hold for any two events
They let expectations be computed without any probabilities

questions.question: Does dependence between events stop a sum of indicators from counting occurrences?
options: Yes, counting requires independent events
Yes, indicators become undefined
No, the sum counts occurrences outcome by outcome
No, because dependence makes all indicators equal one

questions.question: If no event among $A_1,\ldots,A_5$ occurs, what is $\sum_{i=1}^5 \mathbf 1_{A_i}$?
A student treats $\mathbf 1_A$ as equal to $P(A)$ on every outcome. What is wrong?
options: It equals $P(A)$ only on outcomes in $A$, and $0$ elsewhere
It equals $1/P(A)$ on $A$ and $0$ on the complement
Nothing, since $E[\mathbf 1_A]=P(A)$ makes them equal
The indicator is outcome-dependent and equals $0$ or $1$
